speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, each year, on the eleventh day of the eleventh month, Canada pays tribute to the memory of her heroes of two generations who laid down their lives in the cause of freedom. Three times this century, Canadians went off to war to defend our basic aspirations, freedom and peace. Tomorrow will be a time of remembrance. Once again across this vast land we shall honour Canada's heroes of two world wars and the Korean conflict, recognizing the sacrifices they made.
Tomorrow is a very special day, for another reason: November 11, 1978, marks the sixtieth anniversary of the armistice which ended what they called the war to end all wars.
I should like to take a moment to tell hon. members of the House that this morning I met upward of 100 First World War veterans whom I brought here for a special occasion this year; to take part in ceremonies at the monument, to attend a state dinner and various functions such as that. Among that group was a gentleman who will be 108 years old on November 19. He is from Elk Lake, North Bay, Ontario. His health is exceptionally good.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
He had just finished a 20-minute interview on the radio before I left.
Nearly one in every ten Canadians who fought in that First Wcrld War did not return home. More than 50,000 lie in the war cemeteries of France and Belgium. Others found their earthly resting place in graves in the United Kingdom, in the Near East, in north Russia and Siberia, or in native Canadian soil. Some were lost at sea.
Few members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force were soldiers by profession; the force was largely an army of citizen soldiers. From every walk of life they came to render their service, and those who did not return left their country-our country-the poorer for their loss.
At the outbreak of the First World War, with a population of just over eight million people, Canada was on the verge of attaining nationhood, with a future full of promise. In 1914, as part of the British Empire, we faced the most imposing threat to peace and freedom ever experienced up until that time in history. Our very existence, and that of other peace-loving nations, was threatened by war in Europe. For that reason, as war was declared, a generation of Canadian youth lined up and marched off to defend their nation.
Even after 60 years, the mention of such names as Vimy, Passchendaele, Ypres and Arras evokes memories in the minds of many Canadians. Tomorrow, some will remember the mud, the trenches and the suffering. Others will sadly recall the death of a buddy, a friend, a father, a brother, a son. But Canadians collectively should remember with pride the bravery, the heroism and the great military achievements of our Canadian servicemen and women.
Those of both world wars and the Korean conflict who served and returned home, as well as those who stayed "over there", had an ideal. They served, suffered and died to ensure that Canada's path would be upward, that she would take her place in the world as a great, prosperous and happy nation. Tomorrow, with the poppies in our lapels, as wreaths are laid at our cenotaphs, let us all as Canadians observe a few moments of silence and remember the sacrifice of our war dead. Let us, at the same time, reflect on what they gave their lives for; a Canada united, strong and free. We owe it to all of them to keep it that way.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I pay tribute, on behalf of the official opposition, to this speech and these special people, I would preface my remarks by paying my thanks to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) who early this morning sent me a copy of his remarks. I especially commend those who made it possible that this tribute should be made at the very beginning of the proceedings of this House. We feel, now, that it has a priority which it so justly deserves because we are as close as possible to the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month.
We are, once again, summoned by a most solemn admonition to pause for a moment amid this busy world's activities, to pay silent, moving tribute to the memory, not only of those fallen in battle but also those who faced the ordeal of combat and now lie in hospitals and nursing homes with broken bodies and disturbed minds, who, as someone has said, "limp and grope their way down the corridors of time." In the words of President Lincoln, "The world will little note nor long remember what we say here today".

November 10, 1978
Remembrance Day
By the sacrifice of thousands of young Canadian men and women who put their very lives on the line for king and country, this day has been hallowed far beyond our poor power to further consecrate it.
Canada forged her nationhood with the sacrifice of her sons and daughters on land, on the sea, in the air and at home in field and factory. The debt Canadians owe to that generation of valiant men and women can never be completely and adequately discharged.
However, successive governments, following World War I, have over the intervening years put together a framework of legislation to try to compensate our veterans and their families who gave their all, and lost so much, that we might today live in a land where "freedom slowly broadens down from precedent to precedent". These acts of parliament on behalf of veterans are collectively referred to as the veterans' charter. We are still correcting and replacing old laws and enacting new measures in light of today's lifestyle.
While we on this side of the House continue to press for more improvements, we recognize in the present Minister of Veterans Affairs a man who bears the painful scars of conflict and a man who conscientiously and faithfully works for the welfare of veterans.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TRIBUTES TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN FORCES WHO SERVED IN WARTIME
speechtext:
We also know his activities are limited in this field, and that he has difficulty in convincing certain cabinet colleagues that aid to veterans is the very last place in which spending restraints should be applied. We feel they have their priorities all wrong.
On this Remembrance Day in 1978, therefore, we once again press this government to give all widows of veterans with disability pensions some form of widow's benefit, and to adjust ceilings and other constraints affecting war veterans' allowance to a figure commensurate with today's cost of living. This would be the very best wreath to deposit in memory of our veterans.
In closing, I call upon all Canadians, as they bow before cenotaphs across this land, to renew their covenant in the fallen and carry high the torch of freedom thrown to us, which is also a touch of Canada united from coast to coast.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Lepage will be able to remember, I am sure, many of the promises that were made and how well we,

as members of parliament, have or have not fulfilled those promises over the years.
November 11 should not be considered a holiday, Mr. Speaker. It is a day when we should remember the sacrifice that was made by the young people of Canada from 1914 to 1918, the young people of the generation who made the sacrifice from 1939 to 1945 and, later, the conflict in Korea. The soldiers and servicemen of Canada today are still serving the interests of peace around the world, in many countries. We should remember the sacrifice they are making for us and the reasons why they are willing to make that sacrifice.
Too often, when we watch television today, Mr. Speaker, we see war glamorized. All the uniforms and the movie plots developed around war glamorize it. But war was not like that: for those who served, it was a matter of deprivation and many, many hardships. Those who were able to return gave up much: many paid the supreme sacrifice and did not return.
This is the sixtieth anniversary of that war to end all wars, and it behooves all of us to indicate to young people that the sacrifice that was made, was made to keep Canada a free country; that they made that sacrifice, and they made it freely. They made it in the knowledge that it would be a sacrifice that would not have to be made by people who followed. Our young people should know that, because our veterans will not have paid the price in vain if we are able to ensure that there are no more wars and the problems of the world are settled in a more satisfactory way.
I am pleased that the minister has seen fit to honour 100 of those veterans of the First World War. They are getting older, and they will not be with us very long. I join with the opposition member who indicated that we have an obligation to those who did return, and I congratulate the minister for what he has done in the past. As our veterans of the Second World War and the Korean war reach the age where assistance is necessary, we in Canada have an obligation to repay them. We are not repaying them entirely. We should be repaying them with the idea that they fought in three major wars to make this a free country, a united country. Unless we keep faith with them, we will not be assured of the success of the endeavour which they voluntarily and so expensively undertook on behalf of our nation.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to take part in this tribute. I wish to emphasize, like the hon. minister and my colleagues before me, the human contribution, the sacrifice of these men whose courage stood up even in the face of death itself. It is fortunate that we set aside a day to pay tribute to those who died but also to those who remain and bear the consequences of war. Among them are many handicapped who are a living proof of the atrocities of war. This day gives us a special opportunity, to us who have

November 10, 1978

known war, to repeat to the younger generations that others have made the ultimate sacrifice to ensure their future. I am proud of the special attention that the House of Commons has always bestowed on veterans and their plight. It is my hope that through the coming years we will be able to improve their fate and their condition. Mr. Speaker, as we remember on this day the sacrifices demanded by war, let us all be ever more thankful to God for the gift of peace.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Current reports show that profits of the largest corporations in Canada increased, on average, by 25 per cent to 30 per cent in the first nine months of this year compared with last year.
Will the minister inform the House whether his department is undertaking an investigation into these spectacular profit increases and their harmful inflationary consequences related to recent price increases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PROFITS OF LARGE CORPORATIONS-EFFECT ON INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has, indeed, been some amelioration in the profit picture for corporations. There is absolutely nothing wrong with that. I think corporations need to make profits in order to reinvest. We should see that as an improvement in the Canadian economy. The profits of corporations which are still under AIB guidelines will, of course, be investigated to determine whether the guidelines are being breached. But 1 want to say to the hon. member that when we talk about corporate profits, we have to keep the base in mind. Sometimes an increase of 30 per cent from a very low base does not amount to very much money. The same base is not used when we talk about salaries which increase from year to year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that we now have the support of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration respecting social insurance numbers.
The minister is aware that we have a minimum of 1,381 presently listed information data banks in the federal government. Many of them are in such disparate agencies as the Department of External Affairs and the Canadian Saltfish Corporation. The prime identifier is the social insurance number.
I would like to ask the minister what specific controls he plans to introduce to guard against the interconnection of computers by means of social insurance numbers, which poses a threat to individual privacy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: USE OF COMPUTERS LINKED WITH SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS
speechtext: What about your pay cheque?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: USE OF COMPUTERS LINKED WITH SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very difficult to determine just where the opposition stands on this matter. When we bring in legislation which gives access to these banks by individuals so they know exactly what information the government has, hon. members opposite say that is what they want, but in the next breath they suggest we are being too open. In 99 per cent of the cases, the use of the social insurance number is advantageous to the individual, who can receive cheques, refunds from

the Department of Finance, social insurance benefits and benefits from a myriad of other programs which are in place.
In deference to the hon. member, I too am concerned about data banks. We list them. We indicate what is in those data banks. In cases where ministers have responsibilities for one thing or another-the security of the country or the protection of the reputation of individuals-we want to see to it that everyone does not have access to certain information. We are moving into the computer age. There is a concern which is shared by my colleague, the Solicitor General, and we are looking into this matter to see what can be done to build in as much protection as possible so that individual rights will not be infringed.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: USE OF COMPUTERS LINKED WITH SOCIAL INSURANCE NUMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about preventing the kind of data traffic which is taking place, involving unscrupulous computer manipulators who are misusing this kind of information, as well as potential misuse. Quite apart from the fact that the minister now appears to have endorsed the idea of extending the use of social insurance numbers throughout government agencies-and he appears not to be concerned-what is his attitude with respect to putting curbs on private use of this government-issued number?
Specifically, does he intend either to make a strong statement in this House or to bring forward legislation or guidelines to restrict the use of this number outside government, which is getting to be more and more a factor in terms of getting service at banks and other private establishments?

Having regard to the fact that the capacity of our handling system has not increased since 1973, in spite of the 1974 election promises, and given the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board has predicted that Canada's export potential by 1985 would reach 31.5 tons-that is roughly an increase of 50 per cent over the exports we had last year-that means that the shipping capacity must increase by 50 per cent and by 70 per cent on the west coast, and having regard to the fact that most of the increase in those shipments will occur on the west coast, does the government have an over-all plan, or is the government discussing such a plan to meet the potential targets for 1985?

have another day in which to do that. However, notice which comes to the Chair after that day is not really proper notice within the terms of Standing Order 17(2).
I want to say, however, that the three hon. members from New Brunswick have given me notice of an intention to raise this question of privilege. Although 1 have to say that procedurally I cannot entertain that, all three notices pertain to the following remarks made by the hon. Leader of the Opposition on Wednesday afternoon, and are contained in Hansard at page 928, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that that question is in the character of the attempts to sow fear and indeed sow confusion and almost hatred among Canadians which has become so marked among members of the other side-
[ Translation]
-in both official languages, and perhaps particularly members from New Brunswick who speak from time to time in this House.
Again I say I am procedurally without jurisdiction in this matter because the time has gone by.
I simply want to ask the Leader of the Opposition to reflect on those remarks, and particularly to examine the pages of Hansard with respect to a similar occurrence involving the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) just a few months ago when remarks were made of a similar nature. The Minister of Transport at that time indicated he had made those remarks not concerning members of the House of Commons but, in fact, concerning people outside the House of Commons. After considering the arguments it was my disposition of the matter that the Minister of Transport owed it to the House to be absolutely certain that those remarks were not directed toward any member of the House of Commons.
I cannot require that of the hon. Leader of the Opposition in this particular case because, procedurally, I am without that authority. I simply invite the hon. Leader of the Opposition to examine his remarks in the light of that very clear precedent. In any event, if he wishes to take no action, which he is perfectly free to do, I invite him simply to reflect on that choice and the propriety of the language he used last Wednesday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. LANDERS-REMARK MADE BY LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to bring this matter to the attention of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I think I must say, with great respect, however, that this matter could have waited until the Leader of the Opposition was in the House today, or whenever he is in the House, so that he could have the opportunity of answering.
The situation in which we find ourselves as a result of your intervention in this matter, in the absence of the Leader of the Opposition, is that these remarks and your disapprobation of these remarks, stay on the record. They will be the subject of public comment over the three or four days of the weekend without the Leader of the Opposition having the opportunity to raise a defence.
I say that with respect, but I think it is most unfair of you to the Leader of the Opposition.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. LANDERS-REMARK MADE BY LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION

I deeply resent the last remark of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton that anything I have done is in any way unfair to anyone. I simply pointed out that the hon. member may reflect on those remarks, and that he is perfectly free to do nothing if he wishes, because that is his right.
I deeply resent the remark that that is in any way unfair to any member of the House of Commons. I think 1 had been very careful to treat the Leader of the Opposition, in the circumstances, with great generosity.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would not want you to leave the chamber today having any resentment toward me for any remark that I made in this House of Commons, and so I would withdraw it.

I say that without
equivocation.
My recollection is that the Leader of the Opposition was not in his place. I am sure he will address himself to the remarks that were made and perhaps deal with the precedent you have mentioned which concerned the Minister of Transport.
I want to explain to you, as a member of this House who holds you in considerable respect, that the Leader of the Opposition is not one to show intolerance, and has not shown intolerance. The Leader of the Opposition in many ways is an example to many members of this House of Commons on tolerance.

I want to say to you sir, that I have tried to conduct myself in this House in a responsible way, and I hope you will agree that is the case. I would not want those words to remain. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. LANDERS-REMARK MADE BY LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Order, please. I wanted to make it perfectly clear in what I was saying, for the benefit of the record, that this was the third attempt by members on the government side to raise issue with the remarks made on Wednesday afternoon. 1 have indicated that the manner in which it has been done is not procedurally correct.
I have examined the language used by the Leader of the Opposition on Wednesday afternoon, which is the subject of the complaint. I have not found, and I do not think it is procedurally appropriate for me now to find, that this language was necessarily unparliamentary. I simply made an observation upon which I know the Leader of the Opposition will reflect. I can confirm quite emphatically that his conduct in the House has always been exemplary. In the time that he has been Leader of the Opposition I have never found him to strain the patience of the Chair. On this particular occasion the remark was in response to a question in the middle of a speech. It was not a planned remark and it was, I presume, in response to heckling of some sort which does not show on the record of Hansard.
I simply said I have examined the language. I could not resist the comparison with an earlier occasion. I am simply inviting the hon. Leader of the Opposition to take the opportunity to compare his language with that used on a previous occasion which was the subject of a complaint, and take whatever action he sees fit, which in the circumstances I say may be no action at all. In any case, I simply wanted to bring it to his attention.
If I was in any way condemning him in the language that I used, I want to withdraw from that position because I was not making a final judgment on it at all. On some occasions, several occasions in the past, I have simply said to members when they have made a remark in the heat of debate that they might want to reflect on the use of that language. That is an indication that it may be something close to unparliamentary language which they would want to avoid in the future. It may also be language which they would want to explain to the House and, perhaps, withdraw. I do not know. In any case, I am simply saying that out of caution, as we always attempt to exercise ourselves on the side of decorum in the House of Commons. All I am suggesting is that the Leader of the Opposition would want to examine those words and, perhaps the next time he is in the House, make some comment on them.

Privilege-Mr. Francis

subtopic: MR. FRANCIS-CANADIAN PRESS REPORT ON AUDITOR GENERAL'S ANNUAL REPORT
MR. FRANCIS-CANADIAN PRESS REPORT ON AUDITOR GENERAL'S ANNUAL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege arising out of a Canadian Press report concerning the timing of the Auditor General's report. The Canadian Press report, which was carried in the Gazette and the Toronto Globe and Mail, suggests that the Auditor General deferred the tabling of his report from November 21 to November 23 because of pressure from government members. In fact the press report goes on to say, quoting the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers):
-It is clear the government does not want any criticism of its finances to come to light during the budget debate.
There can be no greater distortion of the facts.
The Auditor General announced that in view of the importance of his report, on the one hundredth anniversary of his office, and in his opinion the most important report to proceed from the office in its entire period of existence, it would be subject to special provisions. Hon. members of this House are invited to attend the lock-up session starting at ten in the morning. The committee will sit at 3.30 in the afternoon of the day of tabling.
As a member of the committee and vice-chairman, senior from this side of the House-I am quoting now from the transcript of the committee-I said:
Mr. Chairman, could I interrupt to make an observation . . . This may be relevant to the Auditor General. The Minister of Finance has announced a budget on November 16. The budget debate will be in its third day, the day we will be tabling the public accounts. I wonder if this will in any way affect the timing of the tabling of the Auditor General's report.
The Auditor General went on to say:
-I always feel that when the report is ready it is my duty to deliver it to the Speaker. As to whether that will be an appropriate day for the arrangements that you have asked at the previous meeting I would leave that entirely to the committee. In other words, if you were to advise me that would not be an appropriate day for the committee, who obviously have an interest in this matter, to carry out the arrangements that were described by you the other day then I would certainly like to reconsider the date that I would submit it.
It is an affront to the Auditor General to suggest pressure in any way. Those of us who know the man, know very well that he would never be influenced by pressure from members on any side of the House.
It was clear to those of us who are members of the committee that there is a considerable overlap between the membership of the public accounts committee and those who hope to participate in the budget debate. Frankly, we could not see how we could guess the kind of attendance at the lock-up and the participation at the committee session that was planned for 3.30 that afternoon at a time when there was priority given in the House to the budget. We simply called that to the Auditor General's attention.
The matter was referred to the steering committee and was considered later. I am sure reference to the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), would amply confirm these facts. The committee asked the

Auditor General if he would be prepared to advance the date of this tabling to November 14. After reflection, he felt that he was not in a position to do so. It was then unanimously agreed at the steering committee, at which the hon. member for Red Deer was present, that a more appropriate day might be Thursday, November 23. The Auditor General, after conferring with his staff, decided that he would perhaps make that recommendation and, sir, it comes into your hands when he lays his report before you.
I want to repeat that the only consideration was the convenience of the members of the House in order that the very important report of the Auditor General could receive the attention that it deserves from members on both sides of the House. There was never at any time any suggestion of political motivation or any pressure put on the Auditor General, who is a man, very much his own man.

subtopic: MR. FRANCIS-CANADIAN PRESS REPORT ON AUDITOR GENERAL'S ANNUAL REPORT

But certainly the hon. members on our side most directly responsible for this, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), gave me an entirely different version of what had happened at that meeting. Order, please. I think probably we have gone fairly far on this matter, which is essentially a grievance by members of the House of Commons about an erroneous press report. I do not know that the Auditor General needs any more defence in respect of this. In any case I am not sure there is any question of privilege involved. The matter has been contributed to on both sides. If, when they return to the House, they have any contributions to make to this, I will be only too glad to hear them in the interest of fairness. But I think, so far as the matter has gone this morning, it really ought not to go any further at this time.

subsubtopic: MR. LANDERS-TIMING OF NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wish to point out to Your Honour that my respect for the Chair is monumental, but I find myself
Point of Order-Mr. Landers
suffering from a degree of confusion. The first time I learned of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was at approximately 2.50 p.m. on November 9, 1978. I sent your office notice by hand at approximately 5.10 p.m. the same day.
In my four years of service in this House of Commons, I have only raised one question of privilege. On that occasion Your Honour ruled that notice given at the first available opportunity was suitable to satisfy the rules. The time lapse on the previous occasion was considerably longer than the time lapse in this particular case. I therefore wonder if Your Honour can help me clear up my confusion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. LANDERS-TIMING OF NOTICE RESPECTING QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE
speechtext:
I will be glad to do so. I attempted to do that yesterday for the benefit of the two other members who endeavoured to give notice. Both members endeavoured to give notice to me yesterday during yesterday's sitting of an event that took place in a previous sitting.
Standing Order 17(2) will indicate that notice must be given one hour before the sitting in which it is intended to raise the question. I have always tried to intrepret that order generously in order to accommodate members where reference is made, for example, to a particular member when at the time the reference is made he is away from Ottawa, and upon his return to Ottawa takes up the matter at the first available opportunity.
I would only reasonably interpret that rule to mean that questions of privilege which arise as a result of remarks which are part of the record, and part of the debating record here, must either be raised during the sitting in which they are put forth on the record or, according to Standing Order 17(2), raised in the following sitting, provided, of course, that notice is given to the Chair within the terms of Standing Order 17(2). That means the Chair receives notice of the intention to raise the question of privilege one hour before the sitting on the following day. That has always been extended to members.
In this particular case, I received two notices of an intention to raise this question yesterday, which I would have permitted except that the notices were not received in time. The hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Landers) gave me notice today of his intention to raise this question which arose out of Wednesday's proceeding. I therefore find that that notice is too late.
Granted, as I said today, I was taking a strict line in respect to the interpretation of that, but I think I have to do that. That is the explanation the hon. member was seeking.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, November 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-14, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening in the second reading debate on Bill C-14 I made a few opening remarks. I think it is wise to go back and capsulize some of the points I was making.
First, I said that the problem in Canada is not fiddling with the Unemployment Insurance Act, trying to tighten it up. The problem is not people, but rather jobs. I said last evening that the government, through Bill C-14, has chosen to scapegoat the unemployed, that since it is bereft of any solution to the unemployment problem, the next best thing is to pick on the victims of unemployment. In other words, the government is making the unemployed the scapegoat for its inadequacies with regard to planning the economy so that it may grow and stimulate the creation of jobs necessary for those who want to work.

November 10, 1978

The other point, which is quite important, is that the government has ignored its own studies and statistics compiled by departments of government. For example, I quoted from the latest statement by the Economic Council of Canada to the effect that the problem is not unemployment insurance, but in effect the whole question of employment and what the government ought to do is busy itself with re-energizing the economy of Canada.
I also pointed out that Statistics Canada informs us that on a day to day basis there are only about 40,000 jobs. That includes full-time, part-time, and casual jobs. The latest figure of the number of persons unemployed, on a seasonally adjusted basis, was 901,000 people seeking work in this country.
I want to refer to the Manpower office in Toronto. In yesterday's Toronto Star there was an article written by Carola Vyhnak entitled "Job-hunting Help? It's Off The Wall". It points out that as at the end of September, 1978, there were 12,298 vacancies listed with the metro area Manpower office. At the same time there were 110,281 jobless clients registered with that office. Therefore, even in an area where there is a much greater chance of getting employment, the number of people seeking work through the minister's office exceeds five to one the number of vacancies available.
The last statement of the article is rather interesting. I quote:
Recently a pizza parlour put in an order at one office for 145 positions. More than 1,000 applied.
That is the story across the country. There are too few jobs available for those who are seeking employment.
What does the minister do in Bill C-14 of which he is so proud he trumpets it in the House of Commons? He says this bill will remove 250,000 people from the unemployment insurance rolls. Where will they go? They will go onto the welfare rolls of the provinces and municipalities. Bill C-14 does not deal with the problem, only the symptom.
As I was pointing out last night, this bill was designed on the philosophy held by too many people that when a crime is committed the victim is to blame. One might call it the rape victim syndrome. You blame the victim for the predicament in which she finds herself.
This is a vicious bill, because not only does it discriminate against the unemployed generally but it specifically picks out women from among the unemployed. As I pointed out last night, women are usually the last to be hired and the first to be fired, so the amendments dealing with re-entry into the work force and the repeating of claims within a year can only make it even more difficult for women, who already find they are discriminated against when it comes to securing and retaining employment. It is all part of the scapegoat process.
The government was telling us last year that the reason the program was in trouble was because too many women and
Unemployment Insurance
young people were collecting benefits. This measure is the fulfilment of a search for scapegoats which has been taking place in the last couple of years. If the minister would examine the facts he would see that the relationship between women as workers and women as recipients of unemployment insurance has been declining since 1972.
I turn, now, to consider another group which is being "scapegoated" in this bill. I refer to the youth group. The government is asserting that young people have only a marginal attachment to the work force and that they are abusing the unemployment insurance program. In many respects young people are in the same situation as that in which women find themselves. In other words, they are among the last to be hired and the first to be fired. Since they are just entering the work force they have little seniority and are extremely vulnerable to lay-offs. For example, I know that when Inco cut down its labour force those with less than two years' experience were all laid off.
Thousands of young people who enter the work force every year have very limited work force experience. Many of them find it very hard to get work at all. Yet in spite of the difficulties they face, these young people are actually under represented on the unemployment insurance rolls. This is an interesting point. Young people make up 43.2 per cent of the unemployed, yet they account for only 18 per cent of unemployment insurance claimants.
If ministers looked at their own statistics they would find that young people are not out to rip off the unemployment insurance program. If they looked at their own Statistics Canada figures they would find that young people leave their jobs at the same rate as older workers. Roughly one half of both groups left their previous employment because they were laid off. These people need the same protection as older workers and ought not to be discriminated against.
The changes in unemployment insurance legislation over the last few years, particularly the amendments before us, are going to hurt students. In the past, a student who found work for one summer would have been eligible to draw on unemployment insurance the following summer while looking for permanent or temporary work. That is no longer the case. From now on students who graduate, or who must look for work in the summer, will be left to rely completely on their own resources. As we know, in an economy beset by such high unemployment, those resources today are pretty slim. With only one permanent job for every 20 people seeking it, the graduate will face the same problem as other workers, except that he will be unable to draw from the unemployment insurance fund into which he had paid the previous summer. The person who wants to go back to school will also face problems. There are few enough summer jobs available, yet at the same time the government is cutting back on funding to post secondary education.
Even in the face of its own evidence, the government is trying to convince us that young people and women are cheats and leeches on society. In an endeavour to avoid being blamed for the lack of jobs in the economy, ministers are trying to

November 10, 1978
Unemployment Insurance
convince us that young people really do not want to work. My party, Mr. Speaker, prefers to believe the findings of the study published in 1975 for the Department of Manpower and Immigration, "Canadian Work Values, Findings of a Work Ethic Survey and Job Satisfaction Survey". This study found that Canadians have a very strong motivation to work and that young people and women have exactly the same attitudes as older people and men. These people want to work, and the government, which in the past has followed a policy of creating unemployment, in denying them the opportunity. Now an attempt is being made to deny them even minimum protection under the unemployment insurance program.
I have already mentioned the position of women and young people. The bill before us also discriminates against those whose attachment to the work force is marginal. In times of high unemployment, trades people such as carpenters, electricians, and plumbers, are very susceptible to changes in the unemployment insurance program. The changes contemplated by the government will act as a disincentive. Suppose, for example, that a carpenter in the Ottawa area has the prospect of a job which will last only four or five weeks. These amendments might very well constitute a disincentive to taking a job which might only last for a short period.
There is also in the bill a provision which would discriminate against persons who are not in long-term jobs. For example, there is a requirement which says that in the case of part time work it will be necessary to be employed 20 hours a week to be considered as "attached" to the work force. Formerly the requirement was for a minimum earning capacity of $48 a week.
In an area like the one I represent, which at the moment is experiencing 11.2 per cent unemployment-that is the official figure; it is up to the figure experienced in the Atlantic region-women and young people who may have been selling on a part-time basis, working in a store, are now not even able to get two days of work. This is because the depression in the economic conditions in the area is resulting in retail sales cuts. Employers will have to cut back work formerly available to these people. Many are greatly concerned about the new requirement which will call for 20 hours of work a week. They will not be able to get that number of hours of employment in order to qualify.
The new provisions also discriminate against those in the work force who are in seasonal types of occupation. As well as being unfair to the people with marginal attachment to the work force, women and youth, they are also unfair and discriminatory to some of the regions in Canada. When the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) first announced the changes, he was flailing around looking for some popular policies to follow this fall. His first announcements suggested that the amendment dealing with repeaters would affect all provinces, not just those with below 11.5 per cent of unemployment. That kind of amendment would have disqualified most of Newfoundland's fishermen and would have cost the Newfoundland economy $11 million. Now the legislation is before us we see the government has changed its

mind on that. It will exempt areas with devastating unemployment as opposed to areas with just plain awful unemployment.
What was the rationale for suggesting the 11.5 per cent figure? Any area with 11.5 per cent unemployment or more will be exempt from the provisions regarding repeating claims. What is the difference between 11.5 per cent and 11.2 per cent? I suggest that an area like the Sudbury basin which has 11.2 per cent unemployment is just as hard hit as an area which has 11.5 per cent unemployment. The region I represent will be discriminated against, and the effects of unemployment will be just as devastating as it will be in regions which are arbitrarily exempted.
I am sure the government would like us to believe that it made this decision out of concern for people in high unemployment areas, but I do not see how it can claim that. I think the by-elections which were coming up were good reasons. The minister did not consult the provinces regarding effects. He did not consult the trade union movement or representatives of labour. There were no consultations whatsoever. At the beginning of September the minister made a knee-jerk statement, but he had to backtrack.
Last night in the House he told us that he had been advised by Liberal backbenchers, but the fact is that his bureaucrats proposed this program. The minister announced it without proper consultation. There was a knee-jerk reaction to the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that there would be cutbacks, but it was not properly thought out. Now the minister is backtracking, and I think that the reality of a certain by-election is one of the major reasons for his backtracking.
The fishermen in Atlantic Canada were petitioning. They were all up in arms. There were over 20,000 of them, and the government could not resist that kind of pressure. It seems to me that this is not a very well thought out program. Atlantic Canada will not get off scot-free with respect to the effects of these amendments, because cutting back insured benefits from 66% per cent to 60 per cent will cost the Newfoundland economy $18 million. Newfoundland has the highest unemployment rate in the country. I cannot understand why the federal government would remove that amount of money from an economy which needs every penny it can get. Areas with high unemployment and people who find it difficult to find work will be hardest hit by this bill, but so will other areas.
The chairman of metro Toronto has said that the cutbacks will cost the metro Toronto welfare scheme an additional $10 million. If $10 million more is spent on welfare in metro Toronto, that money has to be taken from other programs which may have a higher priority with the local people. The metro chairman said that the changes would put another 2,500 people on the welfare rolls in metro Toronto, which would eat into other programs. It is clear that these changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act have nothing to do with the economy but everything to do with the government's trying to win back popularity. The government thinks there is a right-
November 10, 1978

wing mood in this country. It is trying to ride that right-wing mood by bringing in this kind of retrogressive legislation rather than coming to grips with the serious economic problems we have.
The solution is to order the economy in such a way as to create the jobs needed by those who are looking for work. The government is playing the old shell game. The 250,000 people affected by this measure will not disappear. The facts we have put on the record indicate that 250,000 people may not qualify for benefits as a result of the changes the minister has brought forward, but that does not mean they will not have the same economic needs they had when they were on unemployment insurance.
They will find themselves going on welfare rolls, or they will steal. In my area there is a study under way which indicates that there is a distinct correlation between crime and high unemployment. The crime rate clearly increases with the unemployment rate, so this is not just an economic problem. That is what this government would have us believe. It is also a very serious social problem with which the government refuses to come to grips.
The Social Planning Council of metro Toronto conducted a study entitled "The problem is jobs, not people". The government uses its energy dealing with the unemployed. It seems to have a titanic philosophy: women and children first. The government seems to be applying that philosophy to the Unemployment Insurance Act. Why does it not use its energy to come to grips with some real problems? Just yesterday in the Toronto Star an article written by Richard Gwyn appeared under the headline "Foreign Firms Blamed for Loss of 200,000 Jobs in Canada." Richard Gwyn wrote:
Foreign-owned branch plants have cost Canada up to 200,000 jobs, a just-published Science Council study states.
The government's own agency, the Science Council of Canada, under Dr. Shepherd, has pointed out that foreign ownership has cost us 200,000 jobs since 1972. That is a problem on which the government ought to expend its energy. It should be dealing with the effects of foreign ownership on the Canadian economy vis-a-vis jobs. Why does the government not use its energy to come to grips with the problems caused by multinational mining corporations in Canada?
Last fall International Nickel laid off 2,600 people in the Sudbury Basin. This government could only wring its hands. It said it could not interfere, that it did not know what to do and that there was no solution but to put these people on unemployment insurance. The government should be coming to grips with the problem of the exploitation of non-renewable resources in Canada. Why is the government not doing so? The government seems to be tying up the House of Commons and the energies of the Department of Employment and Immigration by fiddling with the Unemployment Insurance Act. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think if anyone is seriously looking to see the difference between Liberal and Conservative philosophies, this present debate is an excellent example of the difference between us. I have been reading the debate in Hansard of yesterday, and I believe some of the statements by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) were absolutely punitive. If that is the idea behind unemployment insurance, then it is wrong.
The unemployment insurance system is not a punitive system; it is a system which is supposed to help those people who, through no fault of their own, have lost their jobs. It is a program of temporary assistance until such time as they do find other jobs appropriate to their talents, and certainly with sufficient money to cover their basic and just needs.
What has happened in this regard? I suggest that by innuendo and insinuation on the part of members of the official opposition, helped unfortunately by many members of the media, there has been such a hate campaign conducted against recipients of unemployment insurance that genuine recipients of benefits are now in a corner, almost afraid to admit that they receive benefits. To disparage an entire community of people for the sake of a few abusers is, to me, unethical and dishonest.
Let me refer to some of the points raised so far in the debate. I start by referring to one statement that I consider as being almost cause for a question of privilege. 1 quote a statement by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra last night as reported at page 987 of Hansard. He stated:
We are straightforward people on this side of the House-
To imply that the only straightforward people in this House sit on that side is absolutely and grossly unfair and untrue. I can assure that hon. member, and any other members who share his views, that there is no monopoly held by any party in this House in respect of being straightforward.

November 10, 1978
Unemployment Insurance
The hon. member also seemed to imply that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) wanted to save money, but for what purpose he was not sure. I can tell the hon. member, because the minister made it very clear in his statement last night when he said that the savings are to be applied to other more productive programs. This is a most valid point, and one which warrants support of this House in respect of this program. What the government is trying to do is weed out the abusers who, I repeat, are in the minority, and put the money that is saved to much more constructive use, particularly in the creation of jobs.
There is another point I would very much like to underline, and here again I am referring to what was more or less an innuendo, but extremely dangerous and insidious. To quote again from that hon. member of the Tory party:
This year across Canada there were 150,000 unemployment insurance cheques that were not picked up at special distribution centres during the postal strike. Of course, the government has explanations for this.
Of course the government has explanations for that, Mr. Speaker, yet by innuendo the hon. member is impugning the integrity of thousands of innocent beneficiaries of the unemployment insurance scheme who, for one reason or other, mostly legitimate, I am pretty sure, could not pick up their unemployment insurance cheques during the postal strike. Let me give you an example. It could very well be that many of those cheques were in respect of maternity benefits. I can guarantee that if you are expecting a baby within a few weeks you are not going to run around Toronto trying to pick up your cheque. You just simply cannot do that. That is impossible.
Some of these cheques could have been for sickness claims, and some of them may have been, as the minister replied in answer to a question in the House, payable to people who had already found other jobs. They would be entitled to the cheques, but now could they leave their new jobs to go down and pick them up?
This is the kind of insinuation which, unfortunately, has been spread throughout Canada, and this has caused, yes, invited, hatred and distrust.
If there is one thing that Liberal philosophy supports it is the absolute and vital necessity for a sufficient amount of mutual trust between human beings. I am very proud of the fact that the Liberal government first asks questions, finds out the facts and, if necessary, will punish. To punish the innocent before questions have even been asked is totally unfair and disparaging. These are the kind of attacks which, unfortunately, have led what is essentially a good system into tremendous disrepute. This has caused real beneficiaries of the system to be almost ashamed to admit they are collecting unemployment insurance to which, by the way, they are entitled. The abusers are few and, through good controls, they will be caught. As a result of provisions in this bill many of them will be caught, but perhaps not all.
No one, least of all the minister, is going to pretend that the system is perfect. If it were not so good there would not be so many people trying to abuse it in the first place. There are

some abusers because of human nature. We must admit there are some abusers and we have to do our best to get at them, but in getting at them we must do our best not to hurt the innocent.
There was another point in the hon. member's speech which I am sure the youth of Canada will be interested to study. I refer to the hon. member's statement that there is now a generation of Canadians who have no incentive to work. That is a shameful statement and implies that the youth of Canada does not want to work and has no incentive. That is absolutely shameful and is an attack which should not be allowed to continue.
Let me quote yet another statement. He said that there are "any number of employers . . . having great difficulty in finding workers to fill the jobs". First, I would like to know to what kind of jobs the hon. member has reference. I myself was very recently at an employment centre in Toronto and asked if there were any vacancies there. I was told there were, and I asked what type. I was informed that most were very menial jobs. Unfortunately on that particular day the people looking for jobs were people with high qualifications.
What are we trying to do, and what is the Tory philosophy in that kind of situation? Are we, on the one hand, to encourage our children to stay at school acquiring increasingly higher education, and then when they have made the sacrifice of years at school, are we asking them to accept jobs as dishwashers? Is that all the hope we are offering the youth of Canada?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: There is nothing wrong with washing dishes.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
There is nothing wrong with washing dishes, but I think we should be honest in all our policies. We have no right to encourage the children of Canada to stay in school to become overqualified and to give them unrealistic expectations. It is our duty as a society to provide jobs which will in some ways satisfy those children. We cannot expect them, after they have spent all those years obtaining an education, particularly a higher education, to take on jobs as dishwashers. It is absolutely wrong. As I said, my understanding of the situation in Toronto is that there were vacancies and jobs to be filled, but they were of a more menial type such as dishwashers, or short order cooks.
I wish that the opposition would clarify their position. An hon. member on the opposition side has suggested that the aim of Liberal government policy is to have more and more state intervention. On the one hand we are accused of having more and more state intervention, and on the other hand we are accused by the same party of not doing enough to create employment. They cannot have it both ways. I myself lean toward free enterprise, but I realize that there are times, particularly in a mixed economy such as ours, when the government must intervene. I do not say that it should be done in every instance, but if the private sector is not taking up the slack then government must step in.
November 10, 1978

The Liberal government has taken some very constructive steps in this regard. As an example I cite in particular a report by the second tier committee on policies to improve Canadian competitiveness. This committee was a tremendous breakthrough inasmuch as it was made up of members from the Canadian Labour Congress, representatives of private industry, and officials from the provincial and federal governments. The objective of this conference was not to listen to empty rhetoric, but to examine the whole economic situation of Canada and explore how the situation of job creation could be improved. The report, under the heading "Manpower and Labour Relations", at page 14 reads:
Manpower policy should be, in the view of the committee, a full employment policy. It should be a policy that endeavours not only to ensure industry with a labour force necessary to meet its needs but also aims at providing the individual Canadian worker with the opportunities to improve his or her level of skill, encourages mobility, and enables the individual to have a more fulfilling and satisfying work experience.
It would be interesting to contrast that quote with some of the statements to which I have referred, in the speech made last night.
Having said that, I would like to state to the House, and to the minister who is present in the House, some of my own reservations. I feel that the bill is an honest attempt to stop the few abuses made against the program. However, I have some reservations with regard to the section dealing with training allowances. The minister in his speech said, as reported at page 984 of Hansard:
The basic allowance provided to such people is only intended to offset additional costs, such as transportation, incurred in training.
The people in my constituency who most benefit from the manpower training program are the families with one parent, in most cases women. It is usually mothers who have been abandoned by their husbands and who are usually unskilled, scared, and on welfare. This training allowance enables them to upgrade their skills or to learn new ones. They need this help because if we do not get these people off welfare the person or persons who suffer in the end are the children. By cutting down the basic training allowance we are, ipso facto, denying these mothers the right to training programs under manpower. I still have to be convinced, and I am open to discussion, on how we can avoid cutting out these mothers from the training allowance programs and at the same time cut down their allowance. Welfare simply covers their nutritional needs, their rent, and the needs of the children, but it does not cover, for example, baby sitting, which these women would require if they were to attend a training program. These women need help. Their situation can best be described by an old Persian proverb, "Give a man fish and you feed him for a day, but teach him to fish and you feed him for a lifetime."
I am pleased to see that the minister has made reference to on-the-job training programs for youth. The reports which come from my own riding say that the on-the-job programs are the best thing this department has introduced. They are well received by employers and employees. I doubt, however, that the on-the-job program will be of much benefit to lone parents. If she had a proper job, and I am thinking particularly of
Unemployment Insurance
women again, she would not need training and she would not need an allowance. The point is that these mothers need training in order to get jobs.
The on-the-job training program is directed primarily to youth, male or female. I was glad to see that the minister emphasized the fact that these training programs will be open to women, especially in sectors where they have been under represented in the past. It is a step in the right direction. I am not convinced though that by cutting back on the basic training allowance for women that we are doing them a service. In a year or so, I believe that we will be regretting this decision, but, as I said, I am open to discussion and, no doubt, I will hear more on the subject when we reach the committee stage on this bill.
I should like to refer again to the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra last night when he was referring to people who leave their jobs. He said that an additional problem is the precipitous increase in labour turnover. That is also a matter of great concern to us and one that, I think, needs to be discussed outside the parameters of this bill.
Of course it is very unnerving, unsettling, and uneconomic for the country to have people leave their jobs with great frequency. With this bill the government does not intend to tell people they must stay in a job where the working conditions are appalling or where their abilities are not being recognized. It is not the government's policy to impose that on any person who has a grievance in his job and, therefore, must move. What the government is saying in this bill is that if you really have to change jobs because you cannot find your niche, you are free to do so, but not at the expense of other taxpayers who may be gritting their teeth and staying in their jobs a lot longer.
I think this is typical of the Liberal approach being taken in this bill. The idea is to cut out the obvious abusers, not to put money into the state coffers as such but to devote that money to a much more constructive program such as job creation which, I believe, should be the top priority of all of us.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very important bill, probably one of the most important bills to come before the House in this session. It is a difficult bill, and I understand the difficulties of the minister and maybe even sympathize with them. I can practically tell him the kinds of problems he is having in his caucus are not dissimilar to the kinds of problems I am having in my caucus, because that is a fact of life in the country. It is a fact of life that was rather dramatically addressed by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) in his speech when he quoted Disraeli's eloquent description of the two nations-the nation of the haves and the nation of have-nots.
That dichotomy is a fact of Canadian life. It is a more important fact of Canadian life than any other aspect of our national problems, whether national unity, constitutional prob-
1022

November 10, 1978
lems, linguistic problems, or any other. Until we solve the problem of economic disparity we are not going to have a united country. We cannot have unity when we have widespread disparity.
I just heard my friend, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Railton), make a remark, Mr. Speaker. I am glad to see he is in the House today. He is a good friend of mine. I have great respect for him. I hope he is going to participate in this debate, because one of the concerns about this growing problem of nations of haves and of have-nots is that it is no longer a regional problem; it is a problem in the big cities as well as the small cities and in the Atlantic provinces.
It is interesting that the constituency of the hon. member for Welland is in the Saint Catharines-Niagara area, which has the third highest rate of urban unemployment in the country. That is the area that we in the Atlantic provinces look upon as the banana belt of the country. In the pretty, seemingly prosperous cities of Saint Catharines, Welland, Thorold and Niagara Falls, you would wonder why unemployed could be such a problem as to represent the third highest rate of urban unemployment in the country at over 11 per cent. I know the hon. member for Welland is just as concerned about that as I am.

speechtext:
I listened very carefully to the minister's speech. I have to tell him I was disappointed-disappointed because he showed an insensitivity to the subject that is out of character with the minister or my perception of him. He is not a heartless person; he is a compassionate man. In delivering that cold, sterile speech, prepared for him by faceless bureaucrats who really do not have a feel for the subject, he was demonstrating a rather uncharacteristic insensitivity to a subject that touches directly the lives of so many people.
I was surprised at the brevity of the speech. I would have expected he would go into it in more depth and greater detail to lay the problem properly before the House and set the stage for the debate, but he did not. A few things he said rather surprised me. For example, in the context of justifying the changes in the present unemployment insurance bill, he said he was doing so in order that unemployment insurance will not become a way of life. It is not with any sense of pride that I state to this House that l come from a part of the country where, through economic circumstances in many instances, unemployment insurance has in fact become a way of life. It is an economic fact to be reckoned with in the Atlantic provinces, that visible have-not part of the nation.
It is a way of life in the Atlantic provinces, especially Newfoundland, because unemployment has become a way of life in those provinces. It is ten years since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) campaigned in the Atlantic provinces for the election in 1968, and promised to end all this disparity of high unemployment and low incomes. He was going to end it by bringing in a Marshall aid type plan for the Atlantic provinces. We all know what the Marshall plan did for war-torn Europe. As a result of the Marshall plan, today the Deutschmark is the

strongest currency in the world. Europe is prospering with an employment rate that is the envy of Canada. The economic growth rate is the envy of Canada. That is what the Marshall plan did for Europe. We see what United States aid did for war torn Japan. The Japanese yen is now one of the two strongest currencies in the world. Their economy is the envy of the world.
That is what we were promised in the Atlantic provinces in 1968-a Marshall plan type of aid to end the traditional curse of regional disparity which we inherited in 1949 and, which our neighbours in the Atlantic provinces have had to live with for considerably longer. That promise was as rhetorical and empty in terms of its sincerity and intent as the same promise made by the same Prime Minister in the same election campaign with respect to a just society.
The result is that over the last ten years-I can only take ten years because it coincides with the administration of the right hon. Prime Minister-we have had a pattern of rising unemployment in these four provinces. Where there is no permanent employment all anyone can expect is to get a seasonal job in the fishing industry or the forestry industry in the maritime provinces or, perhaps, farming, or the tourist industry. That is the best you can expect. Or, you can look to what I look upon and what many people see as a glorified form of federal welfare, and that is the Canada Works program. That is all there is. There is nothing else to turn to except unemployment. And now the minister wants to take that away. He wants to take that away from our economy without adequate planning and without adequate regard for the consequences of what he is doing.
As for consultation, Mr. Speaker, this is a word this government has thrown out. There was no consultation on this bill, neither was there any consultation on the family allowance bill. One can ask: why should the federal government consult on an area of federal jurisdiction? The answer is: for the simple reason the transfer payments in these social programs are vitally and crucially important to the economy of the four Atlantic provinces. There are the consequences of cutting back on unemployment insurance without consultation. A province may have a debt somewhere between $1 billion and $2 billion and half a million people. It has to go to the money markets of the world every now and then to borrow money to service the debt to keep the current account going. The consequences are horrendous. It means the people who are deprived of this unemployment insurance will have to fall back on provincial welfare. Surely with that kind of a result one would expect that there would be some kind of gradual process in order to ease the economic impact on provinces, such as Newfoundland. Unemployment insurance is a very important part of the economic fabric in that part of the country.
The minister talked about using a scalpel instead of an axe. I think it is probably easier to use an axe without anaesthetic than it is a scalpel, because at least an axe implies a sudden quick cut, a sudden jolt, whereas the scalpel is a precise
November 10, 1978

instrument that has to find its way in a precise fashion. In order to use the instrument, first of all, one has to anaesthetize the patient. What the minister is doing in the Atlantic provinces and parts of Quebec is applying a scalpel without the benefit of anaesthetic. The result is going to be painful, very painful.
It is a paradox of our nation that I, as a member of this House, representing the oldest settled part of this nation, should speak in these terms. We are not a have-not province, just as the Atlantic provinces are not a have-not region. How can a province that has the greatest potential in terms of hydroelectric resources, both developed and undeveloped, be a have-not province in this energy starved world? How can a province that counts within its territorial jurisdiction 67 per cent of the 200-mile economic zone of Canada's east coast, containing within it the most prolific fund of fishery in the world-how can that province be a have-not province in this protein starved world of ours?
How can a province that has underground vast exploited and unexploited mineral resources-to name a few; iron ore, copper, lead, zinc and-be a have-not province? Half of the iron ore produced in this country is produced in the province of Newfoundland. How can that be classified as a have-not province? How can a province be a have-not province with the tremendous timber resources that the province of Newfoundland and Labrador has, undeveloped, waiting to be exploited? How can it be a have-not province? There is something basically out-of-whack. There is something wrong when that kind of a treasure house of unexploited wealth cannot provide an adequate income for a half a million people. It is crazy. It is insane.
I went to Iceland one time. Here is a country which is not dissimilar to Newfoundland in terms of its climate, in terms of the economic factors that are at play there. Iceland has half the population that we have in Newfoundland. They do not have the mineral resources that we have, apart from thermal resources which they use for hot houses and so on, but that is not a big factor. Iceland does not have the energy resources, apart from what they can generate from the natural steam that is in the ground. They do not have the timber resources. All they have is the same fishing industry selling in the same market, with the same products that we have. And yet with that as an economic base they have achieved a higher standard of living than Canada has. Iceland has practically zero unemployment. They do not worry about inflation because a lot of their inflation is imported. But they have virtually zero unemployment. Their fishermen are the elite of the system. They are the elite of the nation. They are rewarded with an income commensurate with that of the mandarins in the public service of Iceland.
Icelanders come to Newfoundland and look at us and what we have, the climate we have which is so similar to theirs. It would surprise hon. members to know that sheep can graze in the eastern part of Newfoundland all year round, and yet we do not have a woollen industry, like they have in Iceland. Icelandic woollens fetch the highest price in world markets.
Unemployment Insurance
Some day, Mr. Speaker, in the not too distant future I will not have to stand in this House-and I hope to be here-and complain about the Government of Canada cutting back on unemployment insurance benefits because it will be almost as academic as it is for some of my colleagues in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
It was not very long ago that Alberta was a have-not province and the nation had to come to the rescue of Alberta. Now they have oil and they are well away. So the minister comes to us and applies the scalpel and he applies it without the benefit of an anaesthetic because to us unemployment has come to be an unfortunate way of life.
Let us take a look at the facts-first of all, long-term unemployment in the Atlantic provinces. The figures I am using are from the minister's own source of statistics, Stats-Can. Newfoundland has, as of the last figures released, 34,000 people unemployed. These are official seasonally adjusted rates, so this figure will be considerably higher than that and I will explain why in a moment. Officially Newfoundland has 13,000 people who have been unemployed for three months or more. This represents 45 per cent of those people looking for work. I can take hon. members to parts of my province where the people have been unemployed for years, apart from the couple of months' work they can get from Canada Works or the couple of months' work they can get in a fish plant or what have you. That long-term unemployment situation stands out like a sore thumb in the Atlantic provinces. Nova Scotia has 12,000 people unemployed for 3 months of longer, representing 38 per cent of those looking for work. In New Brunswick the figure is 12,000 which represents 41 per cent of those looking for work. Now we come to the province of Quebec where there are 104,000 unemployed, representing 41 per cent of the people looking for work. Long-term unemployment because of the mismanagement, the gross mismanagement of the economy by this government, has become a fact of life, and hence unemployment insurance has unfortunately become a way of life.
I wish that the minister, in keeping with the compassion that I know he has, had hesitated before bringing in this bill. I do not believe a bill like this should be introduced during a period of high unemployment. At least it should not apply to an area where unemployment is chronic and long term in nature.
The hon. member for York-South (Mrs. Appolloni) talked about abusers. There are abusers. There are too many people abusing the system. That is because the system has been badly managed. However, for the one person in six who abuses unemployment insurance, why make the other five suffer by tightening it up? That is exactly what is happening.
We have no time for abusers. Neither do we have any time for those who work the system and quit their jobs, come back on unemployment insurance, and it becomes a cycle. I have no sympathy for that kind of person. Anybody who has a job, all things being equal, should be penalized severely if he quits that

There are a number of things about this bill I would like to mention. I would first like to express my surprise with regard to the Stella Bliss case. We have this bill before us with no intention to amend it to reflect the decision of the Supreme Court, the views of the Canadian Human Rights Commission and, indeed, the views of the minister, because he said in his speech last night they intended to take this into account at a later date.
I remind the minister of this because I do not like what is implied in this bill with regard to women. It is not only the Stella Bliss case, but the implication of taking women out of the Outreach program. I will deal with that in a moment. However, getting back to the Stella Bliss case, the Commissioner for Human Rights on November 2 commended the minister. He said:
It is the hope of this commission that your recommendations to cabinet will result in amending legislation being presented to parliament as part of the bill encompassing the changes which you announced on Septemer 1-
If section 46 were amended so that the question of a woman's availability and capability for work were not unilaterally and arbitrarily determined without consideration of her particular circumstances, but was established according to the individual case, section 46 would then become consistent with the principles already accepted in the 1975 amendment to section 30.
Why does the legislation not reflect that fact? We are obviously passing a bill that is not consistent with the Canadian Human Rights Bill. Any woman in Canada will be able to challenge this bill and challenge it successfully. Obviously we are being asked to pass bad law.
Why does the minister tell the House that he intends to amend the bill when it gets into committee? Failure to do so is not good enough. He expects us to give speedy passage to this legslation, yet he just gives us a passing undertaking that this fact with regard to the rights of women, pregnancy and their entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits, is something that the minister intends to correct at a later date. We will have more to say about that when this bill goes to committee.
With regard to the Outreach program, this defies logic. I have yet to see or hear a rational explanation as to why, in this period of unprecedented high unemployment, women are taken out of the Outreach program. A large part of the unemployment in this country is chronic. A large number of the people affected by this chronic unemployment happen to be women, as well as young people, women in particular.
In periods of high unemployment it is always women who suffer most as the natural tendency is to give the job to the man because he is the provider. I suppose that is understandable in a way, but the facts of life are changing. In fact, they have changed. Women, both married and single, are now a part of the work force. Both spouses now work, a situation brought on by inflation, not by choice but out of economic necessity.
We have the situation of the single parent family, a growing part of the Canadian social fabric. There are more and more single parent families in this country, either by choice or

circumstances, by divorce or what have you. Obviously these women have to work. They have no choice.
I believe I have accounted for two thirds of the women in the work force. That leaves one-third who must work in order to provide for themselves. They are as much if not even more affected by chronically high unemployment as their male fellow citizens. However, for reasons which defy logic, the minister decided as an economic move to take women out of the Outreach program.

It would, of course, be possible to try to eliminate abuses by cutting certain categories of claimants or the duration of benefits, or by extending the period of work before claimants become eligible for benefits. But such recommendations could prove harmful to persons most exposed to periodic and genuinely involuntary unemployment-
